# Introduction

This is the HTML export for the Week 3 assignment. We are looking at the **NYPD Shooting Incident Data (Historic)**, which is published by the City of New York. Every row is a shooting incident reported in New York City, with information about when and where it happened, and about the victim and the suspected perpetrator (when known).

The questions I want to answer are:

1. Are shootings in NYC going up or down over the years?
2. Which boroughs have the most shootings?
3. What time of day do most shootings happen?
4. Can I build a simple model to predict whether a shooting ends in a **murder** (death of the victim)?

At the end I discuss possible **bias** in the data and in my own analysis.

# Load the packages

```{r packages}
# Step 1: List the packages I need.
# tidyverse = data cleaning (dplyr) + charts (ggplot2) + reading files (readr)
# lubridate = makes working with dates easy
packages_needed <- c("tidyverse", "lubridate")

# Step 2: Install any package that is not installed yet (only happens once).
for (p in packages_needed) {
  if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(p, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
}

# Step 3: Load the packages so I can use them.
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
```

# Import the data

```{r import}
# The link to the data on the NYC Open Data website
url <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/v3/views/833y-fsy8/export.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD"

# I save a local copy so the project still works if the website changes.
# The download only happens the first time I knit.
local_file <- "nypd_shooting_data.csv"
if (!file.exists(local_file)) {
  download.file(url, destfile = local_file, mode = "wb")
}

# Read the CSV file into R
shootings_raw <- read_csv(local_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Make all column names UPPERCASE with underscores,
# so the code works even if the website changes the letter case.
names(shootings_raw) <- toupper(gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", names(shootings_raw)))

# Look at the size of the data and the first few rows
dim(shootings_raw)
head(shootings_raw)
```

# Tidy the data

The raw data has some columns I do not need (like map coordinates) and some messy values (like `(null)`, `UNKNOWN`, or strange age groups such as `1020`). In this step I:

- keep only the columns I need,
- convert the date and time into proper formats,
- turn the murder flag into TRUE/FALSE,
- replace messy or unknown values with `NA` (R's code for "missing").

```{r tidy}
# The only age groups that are real categories
valid_ages <- c("<18", "18-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+")

# Values that really mean "we don't know"
unknown_values <- c("UNKNOWN", "(null)", "(NULL)", "U", "")

shootings <- shootings_raw %>%
  # 1. Keep only the columns I want to use
  select(INCIDENT_KEY, OCCUR_DATE, OCCUR_TIME, BORO, STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG,
         PERP_AGE_GROUP, PERP_SEX, PERP_RACE,
         VIC_AGE_GROUP, VIC_SEX, VIC_RACE) %>%
  mutate(
    # 2. Turn the date text into a real Date (works for "01/31/2020" or "2020-01-31")
    OCCUR_DATE = as.Date(parse_date_time(as.character(OCCUR_DATE),
                                         orders = c("mdy", "ymd", "mdy HMS", "ymd HMS"))),
    # 3. Pull out the year and the hour of the day (0-23)
    YEAR = year(OCCUR_DATE),
    HOUR = as.integer(sub(":.*", "", as.character(OCCUR_TIME))),
    # 4. Murder flag as TRUE / FALSE (the file may use true/false or Y/N)
    MURDER = toupper(as.character(STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG)) %in% c("TRUE", "Y", "YES", "1"),
    # 5. Make borough names look nicer, e.g. "BRONX" -> "Bronx"
    BORO = str_to_title(BORO),
    # 6. Clean age groups: anything that is not a real age group becomes NA
    PERP_AGE_GROUP = ifelse(PERP_AGE_GROUP %in% valid_ages, PERP_AGE_GROUP, NA),
    VIC_AGE_GROUP  = ifelse(VIC_AGE_GROUP  %in% valid_ages, VIC_AGE_GROUP,  NA),
    # 7. Clean sex columns: keep only M and F
    PERP_SEX = ifelse(PERP_SEX %in% c("M", "F"), PERP_SEX, NA),
    VIC_SEX  = ifelse(VIC_SEX  %in% c("M", "F"), VIC_SEX,  NA),
    # 8. Clean race columns: unknown values become NA
    PERP_RACE = ifelse(PERP_RACE %in% unknown_values, NA, PERP_RACE),
    VIC_RACE  = ifelse(VIC_RACE  %in% unknown_values, NA, VIC_RACE)
  ) %>%
  # 9. Put age groups in a sensible order (youngest to oldest) for charts
  mutate(
    PERP_AGE_GROUP = factor(PERP_AGE_GROUP, levels = valid_ages),
    VIC_AGE_GROUP  = factor(VIC_AGE_GROUP,  levels = valid_ages)
  ) %>%
  # 10. Remove the old murder flag column because I made a cleaner one
  select(-STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG, -OCCUR_TIME)

# Check the result
glimpse(shootings)
```

## Summary and missing data

```{r summary}
# Basic summary of every column
summary(shootings)

# How many values are missing in each column?
colSums(is.na(shootings))
```

**What I noticed:** the victim columns are almost complete, but the **perpetrator** columns (age, sex, race) have a lot of missing values. This makes sense, because many shootings are never solved, so the police do not know who the shooter was. Because of this, I will **not** use the perpetrator columns in my model. I keep them in the data but I treat them carefully.

**Important note:** one row is one **victim**, not one incident. If a shooting has two victims, the same `INCIDENT_KEY` appears twice. When I count *incidents* I use `n_distinct(INCIDENT_KEY)`.

```{r rows-vs-incidents}
# Number of victims (rows) vs number of unique incidents
tibble(
  victims   = nrow(shootings),
  incidents = n_distinct(shootings$INCIDENT_KEY)
)
```

# Visualizations and analysis

## Visualization 1: Shooting incidents per year

```{r viz-year}
# Count unique incidents in each year
incidents_per_year <- shootings %>%
  filter(!is.na(YEAR)) %>%
  group_by(YEAR) %>%
  summarise(incidents = n_distinct(INCIDENT_KEY))

# Draw a line chart
ggplot(incidents_per_year, aes(x = YEAR, y = incidents)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "NYC shooting incidents per year",
       x = "Year", y = "Number of incidents") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r year-numbers}
# Find the year with the most and the fewest incidents (I use these numbers in my text)
peak_year   <- incidents_per_year$YEAR[which.max(incidents_per_year$incidents)]
lowest_year <- incidents_per_year$YEAR[which.min(incidents_per_year$incidents)]
```

**What I see:** the year with the most incidents is **`r peak_year`** and the year with the fewest is **`r lowest_year`**. Shootings went down for many years, then jumped up again around 2020 (the start of the COVID-19 pandemic) before going down again. I cannot say *why* from this data alone — that would need other information.

## Visualization 2: Shootings by borough

```{r viz-borough}
# Count victims in each borough, split by whether it was a murder
by_boro <- shootings %>%
  count(BORO, MURDER)

# Stacked bar chart, with boroughs ordered from most to fewest
ggplot(by_boro, aes(x = reorder(BORO, -n, sum), y = n, fill = MURDER)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey60", "TRUE" = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c("Survived", "Murder")) +
  labs(title = "Shooting victims by borough",
       x = "Borough", y = "Number of victims", fill = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r boro-numbers}
# Which borough has the most victims?
boro_totals <- shootings %>% count(BORO, sort = TRUE)
top_boro <- boro_totals$BORO[1]
boro_totals
```

**What I see:** **`r top_boro`** has the most shooting victims, and Staten Island has by far the fewest. But these are **raw counts**: the boroughs have very different populations, so this chart does not tell me which borough is the most *dangerous per person*. To do that properly I would need population data for each borough.

## Visualization 3: Time of day

```{r viz-hour}
# Count victims for each hour of the day
by_hour <- shootings %>%
  filter(!is.na(HOUR)) %>%
  count(HOUR)

ggplot(by_hour, aes(x = HOUR, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 2)) +
  labs(title = "Shooting victims by hour of the day",
       x = "Hour (0 = midnight, 12 = noon)", y = "Number of victims") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What I see:** most shootings happen late at night and in the early morning hours, and the fewest happen in the morning (around 7–10 am).

## Victim age groups and murder rate

```{r age-murder}
# For each victim age group: how many victims, and what percent died?
age_murder <- shootings %>%
  filter(!is.na(VIC_AGE_GROUP)) %>%
  group_by(VIC_AGE_GROUP) %>%
  summarise(victims = n(),
            murder_rate = mean(MURDER))

age_murder

ggplot(age_murder, aes(x = VIC_AGE_GROUP, y = murder_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Share of shooting victims who died, by age group",
       x = "Victim age group", y = "Percent that were murders") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r overall-murder}
# Overall percent of victims who died
murder_pct <- round(100 * mean(shootings$MURDER), 1)
```

Overall, **`r murder_pct`%** of shooting victims in the data died. Most victims are between 18 and 44, but the chart shows that **older** victims are more likely to die when they are shot.

# Model: predicting whether a shooting is a murder

I use a **logistic regression**. This is a model for a yes/no outcome — here, *was the victim killed (TRUE) or not (FALSE)?* I use only information that is almost always recorded about the **victim** and the **event**:

- borough
- victim age group
- victim sex
- whether it happened at night (8 pm – 6 am)

```{r model-data}
# Prepare the data for the model: remove rows with missing values in the columns I use
model_data <- shootings %>%
  filter(!is.na(VIC_AGE_GROUP), !is.na(VIC_SEX), !is.na(HOUR), !is.na(BORO)) %>%
  mutate(
    NIGHT = HOUR >= 20 | HOUR < 6,   # TRUE if the shooting was at night
    BORO = factor(BORO)
  )

nrow(model_data)
```

```{r model}
# Fit the logistic regression model
murder_model <- glm(MURDER ~ BORO + VIC_AGE_GROUP + VIC_SEX + NIGHT,
                    data = model_data,
                    family = binomial)

# Show the model results
summary(murder_model)
```

The numbers in the summary are on a "log-odds" scale, which is hard to read. If I use `exp()` on them I get **odds ratios**. An odds ratio above 1 means *higher* odds of murder compared with the baseline group (Bronx, age under 18, female, daytime); below 1 means *lower* odds.

```{r odds-ratios}
# Convert coefficients to odds ratios and round them
odds_ratios <- round(exp(coef(murder_model)), 2)
odds_ratios
```

## Checking the model

```{r model-check}
# Add the model's predicted probability of murder to each row
model_data$predicted_prob <- predict(murder_model, type = "response")

# Compare the average predicted probability with the real murder rate, per age group
model_data %>%
  group_by(VIC_AGE_GROUP) %>%
  summarise(actual_rate    = round(mean(MURDER), 3),
            predicted_rate = round(mean(predicted_prob), 3))

# Plot: predicted vs actual murder rate per age group
model_data %>%
  group_by(VIC_AGE_GROUP) %>%
  summarise(Actual = mean(MURDER), Predicted = mean(predicted_prob)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Actual, Predicted), names_to = "type", values_to = "rate") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = VIC_AGE_GROUP, y = rate, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Model check: actual vs predicted murder rate",
       x = "Victim age group", y = "Murder rate", fill = "") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What the model tells me:** victim **age** is the strongest predictor — the older the victim, the higher the odds that the shooting is fatal. The predicted rates are close to the actual rates per age group, so the model captures that pattern.

**Limitation of the model:** most shootings are *not* murders, so if I used a simple "probability > 50% = murder" rule, the model would predict "not murder" almost every time. That means this model is useful for *comparing groups*, but it is **not** good at predicting whether one specific shooting will be fatal. Things that really matter — where the person was hit, how fast the ambulance came, the type of gun — are not in the data.

```{r threshold-check}
# How many shootings would the model call a "murder" using a 50% cut-off?
table(Predicted_murder = model_data$predicted_prob > 0.5,
      Actual_murder    = model_data$MURDER)
```

# Possible bias

## Bias in the data

- **Reporting bias:** the data only includes shootings that were reported to and recorded by the NYPD. Shootings that were never reported are missing.
- **Missing perpetrator information:** a large share of perpetrator age, sex and race is missing because many cases are unsolved. The cases that *are* solved may be different from the unsolved ones, so any conclusion about "who the shooters are" could be very misleading. This is why I did not use these columns in my model.
- **How race is recorded:** race and age are written down by police officers, sometimes based on what a witness says or what the officer thinks. These labels may not be accurate.
- **Policing differences:** some neighborhoods are policed much more than others. More police presence can mean more incidents are recorded there, which can make some areas look worse than they really are compared with others.
- **No population data:** the dataset gives counts, not rates. Bigger boroughs will naturally have more shootings, so comparing raw counts can be unfair.
- **Changing definitions over time:** the way data is collected or classified may have changed over the years, which could affect the yearly trend.

## Bias in my analysis

- **My own expectations:** before starting, I expected certain boroughs and age groups to stand out. To limit this, I let the charts and numbers speak first and I avoided making claims about *why* something happens.
- **My choices:** I decided which columns to keep, which messy values to turn into `NA`, and what counts as "night". Different choices could change the results a little.
- **Removing missing data:** the model only uses rows with complete victim information. If those rows are different from the removed rows, the model could be slightly biased.
- **Sensitive variables:** I chose **not** to include race in my model. Race is recorded unreliably here and using it could reinforce stereotypes without explaining any real cause.

# Conclusion

- Shootings in NYC went down for many years, increased sharply around 2020, and then started to fall again. The peak year in the data is **`r peak_year`**.
- **`r top_boro`** has the highest number of shooting victims, but without population data I cannot say it has the highest *rate*.
- Most shootings happen late at night and early in the morning.
- About **`r murder_pct`%** of victims die. My logistic regression shows that **older victims are more likely to die** when shot, while borough, sex and time of day matter less.
- The data has important sources of bias — especially missing perpetrator data and reporting/policing differences — so these results describe *recorded* shootings, not all gun violence in the city.

**Ideas for next time:** add borough population data to compute rates per 100,000 people, and look at seasons (months) to see if shootings increase in summer.
